body: Across a period: atomic radius generally shrinks (more protons pull the same shell). Metallic character falls; ionisation energy and electronegativity rise. Down a group: extra shells → bigger atoms, easier to lose electrons (metals get more reactive; non-metals less).

body: Atomic number Z = protons = electrons in a neutral atom. Mass number A ≈ protons + neutrons. Period = occupied shells. Main-group number ≈ outer electrons (He sits with the nobles). Na as 2,8,1 already says Group 1, Period 3, ion Na⁺.

Alkali metals soften and melt lower down the group. All give H₂ + an alkaline solution with water; the fizz gets violent. Halogens go from pale gas (F₂, Cl₂) toward darker solids (I₂). A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt (Cl₂ + 2KI → I₂ + 2KCl).
Transition trio for exams: coloured compounds, more than one ion charge (Fe²⁺ / Fe³⁺), catalysts. Noble gases: full shell, used when you want no reaction.

The electron shells consist of one or more subshells that are denoted by the letters s, p, d, and f.
Transitions elements are found in the center of the periodic table and are denoted by a letter B.
The two long rows which are located below the main body of the table are called inner transition elements.

cards.title: How to classify an unknown solid
body: Ask four school tests: melting point high or low? Does the solid conduct? Does the melt/solution conduct? Does it dissolve in water? High melt + conducts only when molten/dissolved → ionic. High melt + never conducts + insoluble → giant covalent. Low melt + never conducts → simple molecular. Conducts as a solid and bends → metal.

Dot-and-cross: metals lose until they look noble; non-metals gain or share until they look noble. MgCl₂ needs two Cl because Mg gives two electrons. Covalent pairs sit between symbols; leftover dots are lone pairs. Lone pairs push — that is why water is bent and ammonia is pyramidal (named properly in Grade 12).

Hydrogen bonding is a special strong intermolecular force, not a fourth primary bond. It explains water’s high boiling point, ice floating, and DNA later. When water boils you break H-bonds between molecules, not the O–H covalent bonds inside a molecule — if you broke those you would make hydrogen and oxygen gases.

body: Always say the temperature when you quote solubility — “35 g per 100 g water at 20 °C” is a complete sentence; “35 g” is not. A solubility curve slopes up for most solids; a point above the curve is supersaturated, on the curve saturated, below unsaturated.
